title: A generic stack
goal: Make the linked stack hold elements of any type with void * and pointers to functions, know who frees what, and remove a node from the middle of a singly linked list safely.

topics.title: A stack of anything: storing void * elements
topics.examNote: Exams ask you to *use* a container like this more than to build one: push the address of a heap object, pop into a `void *` variable, and free each object exactly once. Be ready to say who frees what.

blocks.text:
### The idea: store a pointer to the element

C has no type that can hold a value of *any* type. But it has `void *` (Day 12): a pointer to an object of an unspecified type. Any object pointer converts to `void *` and back without a cast. So the generic node stores a **pointer to the element** instead of the element:

```c
struct node {
    void *elem;           // the ADDRESS of the element, whatever its type
    struct node *next;
};
```

A picture of a stack holding three `double` objects:

```
 stack struct        nodes (heap)                    elements (heap)
 +------+-----+      +------+------+                 +-----+
 | top  |  o--+----> | elem |  o---+---------------> | 4.5 |  a double
 | size |  3  |      | next |  o   |                 +-----+
 +------+-----+      +------+--|---+
                               v
                     +------+------+                 +-----+
                     | elem |  o---+---------------> | 3.0 |
                     | next |  o   |                 +-----+
                     +------+--|---+
                               v
                     +------+------+                 +-----+
                     | elem |  o---+---------------> | 1.5 |
                     | next | NULL |                 +-----+
                     +------+------+
```

Two important consequences:

- The stack **never looks inside** an element. It does not know the element's type or size, so it never copies the element (there is no element size and no copying of bytes in this design). It only copies the *address*.
- Each element must stay alive **at least as long as the stack** holds its address. The notebook: *typically, this means that memory for each element will be dynamically allocated* (with `malloc`, Day 18).

blocks.caption: From qlgstack.c: almost identical to qlstack_push and qlstack_pop. Only the element type changed.

blocks.text:
Note that `pop` frees the **node**, but not the element. After a pop, the element's address is in your variable and the element is **your** job.

### Using it with `double`

Each pushed `double` gets its own heap object. To pop, declare a `void *` variable, pass its address, then convert to the real type (`double *top = p;` needs no cast, Day 12). `qlgstack_print` and `qlgstack_free` take one extra argument (a function); they are explained in the next lesson.

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o doubles doubles.c qlgstack.c
$ ./doubles
s: top : 4.5, 3.0, 1.5 : bottom
popped 4.5
s: top : 3.0, 1.5 : bottom
blocks.caption: Compile your program together with qlgstack.c, as with qlstack. (The notebook's command says qlstack.c: that is a typo, the file is qlgstack.c.)

blocks.q: After `double *d = malloc(sizeof(double)); *d = 2.0; qlgstack_push(s, d);`, what exactly does the new node store: the value 2.0, a copy of it, or something else?
blocks.a: The node's `elem` member stores the **address** held in `d` (converted to `void *`). The `double` itself stays where `malloc` put it; the stack never copies it.

blocks.text:
The notebook's `demo.c` pops with `int *val1; qlgstack_pop(q1, &val1);`. `&val1` is an `int **`, not a `void **`, and gcc warns:

```
demo.c:42:26: warning: passing argument 2 of 'qlgstack_pop' from incompatible pointer type [-Wincompatible-pointer-types]
qlgstack.h:54:44: note: expected 'void **' but argument is of type 'int **'
```

`void *` converts to and from any object pointer, but `void **` is **not** generic: it means "pointer to a `void *` object". Write the clean version: `void *p; qlgstack_pop(q1, &p); int *val1 = p;`

### Element lifetime: one object per element

Because the stack stores addresses, pushing the address of the **same** variable several times gives several nodes that all point at **one** object:

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o samebox samebox.c qlgstack.c
$ ./samebox
top : 4, 4, 4 : bottom

blocks.text: All three nodes hold `&x`. When the stack is printed the loop has finished and `x` is 4, so every element reads 4. (This is well defined only because `x` is still alive. If `x` were a local of a function that had already returned, the nodes would hold dangling pointers: undefined behaviour.) The fix is the `doubles.c` pattern: `malloc` a new object for each element.

blocks.q: Why doesn't the notebook make the stack copy each element into the node, so lifetimes would not matter?
blocks.a: To copy an element the stack would need to know how many bytes it has, and the notebook's stack is designed to know nothing about its elements. Storing only addresses keeps it simple: one `void *` per node works for every type. The price is the lifetime rule: the user must keep each element alive (usually on the heap) while the stack points at it.

blocks.text:
### Key points

- Generic node: `struct node { void *elem; struct node *next; };`. The stack stores **addresses** of elements, never copies.
- `qlgstack_push(s, ptr)` takes any object pointer (it becomes `void *`).
- `qlgstack_pop(s, &p)` with `void *p;`. Then convert: `double *d = p;`. Do not pass an `int **`.
- `pop` frees the **node** only; the popped element is now yours.
- Every element must outlive its time in the stack: `malloc` a separate object for each one. Pushing `&x` repeatedly gives many nodes pointing at one object.

topics.title: Pointers to functions: printing and freeing unknown elements
topics.examNote: Know how to declare a pointer to a function (with and without `typedef`), how to write a small `print_...(const void *elem)` or `free_...(void *elem)` function for a given type, and the table of who frees what.

blocks.text:
### Two new problems

`qlstack_print` printed each element with `printf("%d", n->elem)`. The generic stack cannot do that: it does not know whether `elem` points at an `int`, a `double` or a struct.

`qlstack_free` freed every node. The generic stack also has to deal with the **elements**, but it cannot know how: maybe each one is a single `malloc` block (call `free`), maybe it is a struct holding another heap pointer (free that first), maybe it is not on the heap at all (do nothing).

The notebook's solution: the **user** of the stack knows the type, so the user writes a small function that prints one element, and another that frees one element, and **passes those functions to the stack**. C passes a function by passing a **pointer to a function**.

### Pointer to a function

A pointer to `int` stores the address of an `int` object. A **pointer to a function** stores the address of a function. To declare one, take the function's declaration and replace its name with `(*name_of_pointer)`:

```c
void print_int(const void *elem);           // a function
void (*ptr2func)(const void *elem);         // a pointer to such a function
```

Read it as: `ptr2func` is a pointer to a function that takes a `const void *` and returns `void`. The parentheses around `*ptr2func` matter: without them, `void *ptr2func(const void *elem);` declares a *function* that returns a `void *`.

- Assign: `ptr2func = &print_int;` or simply `ptr2func = print_int;` (the `&` is optional).
- Call: `(*ptr2func)(&a);` or simply `ptr2func(&a);` (the `*` is optional).

The pointer can point at **any** function with that return type and that parameter list. This is the notebook's example (with the optional forms used on the last call):

Each `print_` function converts its `const void *` parameter to a pointer to the real type (no cast needed) and then uses it. `print_string` gets `str`, which is already a `char *` to the first character, so it does not dereference.

### `typedef` for a function pointer type

Function pointer declarations are hard to read. A `typedef` (Day 23) gives the pointer **type** a short name. Write `typedef`, then the declaration with the name replaced by `(*alias)`:

```c
typedef void (*print_func)(const void *elem);
```

Now `print_func p = print_int;` declares the same pointer as `void (*p)(const void *elem) = print_int;`. The short name is most useful for a **parameter**, when you pass a function to a function:

blocks.q: Declare a pointer `fp` that can point at `void free_int(void *elem)`, and make it point there. Then write a `typedef` named `free_func` for that pointer type.

blocks.text:
### Printing and freeing the generic stack

`qlgstack.h` declares the two function pointer types:

```c
typedef void (*qlgstack_print_func)(const void *elem);
typedef void (*qlgstack_free_func)(void *elem);
```

`qlgstack_print(pre, s, post, ptr)` is `qlstack`'s print with optional text before and after, where each element is printed by calling `ptr(n->elem)`. If `ptr` is `NULL`, each element is printed as `?`. The print function takes `const void *` because printing must not change the element.

`qlgstack_free` is `qlstack_free` plus one line:

blocks.caption: From qlgstack.c. If ptr is NULL, the elements are left alone.

blocks.text:
The free function's parameter is `void *`, not `const void *`, because it usually ends with `free(elem)`, and `free` takes a non-`const` pointer.

### Who frees what

| Memory | Freed by | When |
|---|---|---|
| the stack struct | `qlgstack_free` | at the end |
| one node | `qlgstack_pop` | when it is popped |
| the remaining nodes | `qlgstack_free` | at the end |
| an element still in the stack | the free function you pass to `qlgstack_free` (nothing if you pass `NULL`) | at the end |
| a popped element | **you** | after you are done with it |

Pass a free function when the stack holds the **only** pointers to heap elements. Pass `NULL` when the elements are not yours to free (for example `argv` strings or string literals):

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o words words.c qlgstack.c
$ ./words red green blue
top : blue, green, red : bottom

blocks.text:
### Why a function, and not just `free`?

For a struct that holds its own heap pointer, one `free` is not enough. Here each `student` owns a heap copy of its name (Day 20 style), so `free_student` frees the name first and then the struct. Only the user knows this; the stack just calls the function. (To keep the example short, `main` does not check whether `student_new` returned `NULL`.)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o students students.c qlgstack.c
$ ./students
top : Grace(85), Linus(78), Ada(91) : bottom
$ valgrind --leak-check=full ./students
...
==22824==   total heap usage: 11 allocs, 11 frees, 4,224 bytes allocated
...
blocks.caption: 11 allocations: the stack, 3 nodes, 3 structs, 3 names, and one buffer printf uses internally. All freed.

blocks.text:
### The notebook's `demo.c` leaks

`demo.c` pushes heap `int`s onto two stacks, pops them all, and frees both stacks with `free_int`. But by then the stacks are **empty**: the popped elements were never freed. valgrind finds the leak (the `malloc` lines 20 and 21 are the two element allocations):

```
$ gcc -std=c17 -g -o demo demo.c qlgstack.c
$ valgrind --leak-check=full ./demo 1 2 3
...
==25575==     in use at exit: 24 bytes in 6 blocks
==25575==   total heap usage: 15 allocs, 9 frees, 4,248 bytes allocated
==25575== 12 bytes in 3 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 1 of 2
==25575==    by 0x109317: main (demo.c:20)
==25575== 12 bytes in 3 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 2 of 2
==25575==    by 0x109325: main (demo.c:21)
```

The cure is the "popped element: you" row of the table: `free(val1);` and `free(val2);` after printing them.

Passing a free function when the elements are NOT heap blocks (for example `qlgstack_free(s, free_string)` in `words.c`, where the elements are `argv` strings) calls `free` on memory that `malloc` never gave you: undefined behaviour, often a crash ("free(): invalid pointer"). Pass `NULL` instead.

Copy `qlgstack.h` and `qlgstack.c` from `c/src/qlgstack/` and the `doubles.c` program above into one folder. Compile with `gcc -std=c17 -Wall -g -o doubles doubles.c qlgstack.c` and run `valgrind --leak-check=full ./doubles`: it should say `8 allocs, 8 frees`. Then delete the line `free(top);` and run valgrind again: you should see 8 bytes definitely lost.

### Key points

- Pointer to a function: replace the function name by `(*p)`: `void (*p)(const void *elem);`. Assign `p = f;` (or `&f`), call `p(x)` (or `(*p)(x)`).
- `typedef void (*print_func)(const void *elem);` names the pointer type; handy for parameters.
- A print function takes `const void *`, converts it to the real pointer type and prints. A free function takes `void *` and frees everything the element owns.
- `qlgstack_print(pre, s, post, print_fn)`: `NULL` prints `?`. `qlgstack_free(s, free_fn)`: `NULL` leaves the elements alone.
- Who frees: nodes and the stack: the stack code. Elements left in the stack: your free function. Popped elements: you.

topics.title: Removing a node from the middle of a linked list
topics.examNote: The December 2016 final, Q5 (10 marks, a "slightly hard" question on Prof. Ma's list), asked for a function that deletes one particular node from a singly linked list of `int`s, returns its data, frees the node, and does nothing (returns 0) for lists that are too short. The pattern below (walk with `prev` and `cur`, unlink, then free) is exactly what it tests. Writing item c25-w-03 is modeled on it.

blocks.text:
### Worked example: remove 30 from `[10,20,30,40,50]`

**Start.** `prev` is `NULL` (no node before the head), `cur` is the head:

```
 head
  |
  v
 +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+------+
 | 10 | o-+-->| 20 | o-+-->| 30 | o-+-->| 40 | o-+-->| 50 | NULL |
 +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+------+
  ^
 cur          prev = NULL
```

**Walk.** While `cur->elem != 30`: `prev = cur; cur = cur->next;`

| step | `prev` points at | `cur` points at | `cur->elem == 30`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| start | (NULL) | 10 | no |
| 1 | 10 | 20 | no |
| 2 | 20 | 30 | yes: stop |

```
 head
  |
  v
 +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+------+
 | 10 | o-+-->| 20 | o-+-->| 30 | o-+-->| 40 | o-+-->| 50 | NULL |
 +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+---+   +----+------+
                ^             ^
               prev          cur
```

**Unlink.** `prev->next = cur->next;` copies the address of the 40 node into the 20 node's `next`. The list now skips 30, but `cur` still points at it, so it is not lost yet:

```
                              cur
                               |
                               v
                             +----+---+
                             | 30 | o-+--+
                             +----+---+  |
 head                                    v
  |
  v
 +----+---+   +----+---+               +----+---+   +----+------+
 | 10 | o-+-->| 20 | o-+-------------->| 40 | o-+-->| 50 | NULL |
 +----+---+   +----+---+               +----+---+   +----+------+
                ^
               prev
```

**Free.** `free(cur);` returns the 30 node to the heap. The list is `[10,20,40,50]` and nothing leaked. (`cur` still holds the old address, so it must not be used again.)

### The special case: removing the head

If the target is the **first** node, the walk stops at once and `prev` is still `NULL`: there is no node before it whose `next` could change. Instead the **head pointer** itself must move: `head = cur->next;` then `free(cur);`.

Because a function's parameter is a **copy** of the caller's pointer (Day 11), changing `head` inside the function does not change the caller's variable. So the function **returns the new head**, and the caller writes `list = remove_first(list, 10);`. Two other cases need care: the target is not found (`cur` becomes `NULL`: change nothing), and the empty list (`head` is `NULL`: the loop never runs, same as not found).

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o remove remove.c
$ ./remove
[10,20,30,40,50]
[10,20,40,50]
[20,40,50]
[20,40]
[20,40]
$ valgrind --leak-check=full ./remove
...
==22856==   total heap usage: 6 allocs, 6 frees, 4,176 bytes allocated
...
blocks.caption: Middle, head, last, not found. Removing the last node is the middle case with cur->next == NULL, so prev->next becomes NULL.

blocks.text:
`free_list` uses the same idea as `qlgstack_free`: save `head->next` in a variable **before** freeing `head`, because after `free(head)` you may no longer read `head->next`.

### A function that cannot change the head

In the 2016 exam the function's parameter was the list itself (a copy of the head pointer) and its return value was the deleted **data**, not a new head. Such a function can never remove the first node: the caller's pointer would still point at the freed node. That is why the question said that a list too short to have the requested node should be left alone (return 0). Read such conditions carefully: they tell you which special cases to test **first**, before you touch `->next` of a pointer that might be `NULL`.

Freeing first and unlinking second reads a freed node:

```c
free(cur);
prev->next = cur->next;    // reads cur after it is gone
```

Recent gcc even warns (`warning: pointer 'cur' used after 'free' [-Wuse-after-free]`) and valgrind reports `Invalid read of size 8`. The order is always: **unlink, then free**. If you need the data (to return it), save it in a variable before `free` too.

Writing `prev->next = NULL;` to remove a node in the middle cuts off **everything** after it: those nodes are still allocated but no pointer reaches them (a leak). Only for the last node is `cur->next` equal to `NULL`, which is why `prev->next = cur->next;` handles the middle and the end with one line.

blocks.q: `prev` points at the node before `cur`, and `cur` is not the head. Write the two statements that remove `cur` from the list and release its memory.
Why does the walk need `prev` at all? Could we stop at the node before the target by testing `cur->next->elem`?
blocks.a: Yes, that also works (stop when `cur->next != NULL && cur->next->elem == target`, then `cur` plays the role of `prev`). But you must test `cur->next != NULL` first, and the head still needs its own case. The `prev`/`cur` pair is the pattern the course uses and is harder to get wrong: `cur` is always the node you are looking at, `prev` always the one before it.

blocks.text:
### Key points

- Removing a node = **find** (`prev` one step behind `cur`), **unlink**, **free**.
- Middle or last node: `prev->next = cur->next;`. Head: `head = cur->next;` (detected by `prev == NULL`).
- Unlink and save any data **before** `free(cur)`. Never read `cur->...` afterwards.
- A function that may remove the head must return the new head (the parameter is a copy). A function that returns something else must leave the head alone.
- Test the short cases first: empty list (`head == NULL`), one node (`head->next == NULL`), target not found (`cur == NULL`).

flashcards.front: Why can't `qlstack` (from Days 23 and 24) hold `double` values, and what is the cost of copying it for each type?
flashcards.back: Its node has an `int elem` member. Copying the code for every element type is **code duplication**: the same logic in many places, so every fix must be made many times.

flashcards.front: What does a node of the generic stack store?
flashcards.back: `void *elem`: the **address** of the element (plus `struct node *next`). The stack never copies or looks inside the element.
Each element must stay alive at least as long as the stack holds its address. Usually: `malloc` a separate object for each element.
Pop must write a `void *` (the element's address) into the caller's variable, so it needs that variable's address: a pointer to a `void *`. Call it as `void *p; qlgstack_pop(s, &p);`.

flashcards.front: `int *v; qlgstack_pop(s, &v);` gives a warning. Why, and what is the fix?
flashcards.back: `&v` is `int **`, which is not compatible with `void **` (only `void *` is generic). Fix: `void *p; qlgstack_pop(s, &p); int *v = p;`
Only the popped **node**. The element is handed to the caller, who must free it (if it is on the heap) when done.

flashcards.front: Declare `fp`, a pointer to a function that takes a `const void *` and returns nothing.
flashcards.back: `void (*fp)(const void *elem);` (the parameter name is optional). The parentheses around `*fp` are required.
A **function** named `fp` that returns a `void *`. Without parentheses around `*fp` it is not a pointer variable.

flashcards.front: Two ways to call the function that `p` points at with argument `x`.
flashcards.back: `(*p)(x)` and `p(x)`. Likewise `p = f;` and `p = &f;` both make `p` point at `f`.

flashcards.front: Write a `typedef` named `print_func` for a pointer to `void f(const void *elem)`.
Write the print function for a stack of `int` elements.
Why does the print function take `const void *` but the free function `void *`?
flashcards.back: Printing must not change the element, so `const`. Freeing usually calls `free(elem)`, and `free` takes a non-`const` pointer.

flashcards.front: `qlgstack_print(pre, s, post, NULL)` and `qlgstack_free(s, NULL)`: what does `NULL` mean in each?
flashcards.back: Print: each element is printed as `?`. Free: free the nodes and the stack but leave the elements alone.
Stack struct and remaining nodes: `qlgstack_free`. A popped node: `qlgstack_pop`. Elements still in the stack at the end: the free function you pass. Popped elements: you.

flashcards.front: The three steps of removing node `cur` from a singly linked list
flashcards.back: 1. **Find** it, with `prev` one step behind. 2. **Unlink**: `prev->next = cur->next;` (or `head = cur->next;` if `prev == NULL`). 3. **Free**: `free(cur);`
The unlink reads `cur->next`. After `free(cur)` the node's lifetime is over, so reading it is undefined behaviour (use-after-free).

flashcards.front: How do you know, after the walk, that the node to remove is the head?
flashcards.back: `prev` is still `NULL`: the walk stopped before taking any step. Then the head pointer must change: `head = cur->next;`.

quiz.explain: `f` first points at `twice`: `a = twice(3) = 6`. Then `f = square`, so `b = square(6) = 36` and `(*f)(-2) = square(-2) = 4`. `f(x)` and `(*f)(x)` are the same call.

quiz.q: Which line declares `fp` as a pointer to a function like `void free_thing(void *elem)`?
quiz.explain: Replace the function name with `(*fp)`. Option A declares a function `fp` returning `void *`. C and D are not valid declarations.
`apply` calls `f` on every element. `{4,-1,0}` after `add_one` is `{5,0,1}`, after `negate` `{-5,0,-1}`, after `add_one` again `{-4,1,0}`.

quiz.q: This program is compiled with the notebook's `qlgstack.c`. What does it print?
quiz.explain: The stack stores **addresses**. The bottom and top nodes both hold `&a`, the middle one `&b`. When printing, `a` is already 10, so both `&a` elements read 10. Nothing was copied at push time.

quiz.q: This program is compiled with the notebook's `qlgstack.c`. What does it print?
quiz.explain: Pushing Mon, Tue, Wed makes Wed the top. Pop gives back the address of "Wed" in `p` and leaves 2 elements. With a `NULL` print function, every element prints as `?`. `pre` and `post` are printed around the stack. `qlgstack_free(s, NULL)` is right here: the strings are string literals, not heap blocks.

quiz.q: Write the lines that pop the top element of the generic stack `s` (it holds heap `double`s), print it with `%.2f`, and release its memory. Use no casts.
quiz.explain: Pop needs the address of a `void *` variable. `void *` converts to `double *` without a cast. The popped node is freed by pop, but the element is now yours, so `free(d)` after the last use.

quiz.q: A generic stack holds pointers to heap `struct box { int *values; size_t count; }` objects, where each `values` array was also `malloc`'d. Write `void free_box(void *elem)` for `qlgstack_free`.
quiz.explain: Convert to the real type first. Free what the struct owns (the array) **before** the struct itself: after `free(b)` you may no longer read `b->values`. Just `free(elem)` would leak every array.

quiz.q: A program pushes `argv[1]`, `argv[2]`, ... onto a `qlgstack`. How should it release the stack at the end?
options: pop every element and call `free` on each
quiz.explain: The `argv` strings were not allocated with `malloc`, so they must not be freed. `NULL` frees the nodes and the stack only. `free(s)` alone leaks every node, and options A and D call `free` on non-heap memory (undefined behaviour).

quiz.q: The notebook's `demo.c` frees both stacks with `free_int` at the end, yet valgrind reports `definitely lost: 24 bytes in 6 blocks` for `./demo 1 2 3`. Explain the leak and how to fix it.
quiz.answer: Every element is popped before the stacks are freed, so `qlgstack_free` finds empty stacks and `free_int` is never called. The 6 popped heap `int`s (3 per stack, 4 bytes each) are never freed. Fix: `free(val1);` and `free(val2);` after they are printed in the pop loop.
quiz.explain: Pop frees only the node; a popped element belongs to the caller.

`add_front` puts each new value in front, so the list is `[16,9,4,1]`. Removing 4 (middle) gives `[16,9,1]`; removing 16 (the head, `prev == NULL`) gives `[9,1]`; 5 is not found, so nothing changes. The loop prints the remaining elements one per line.

quiz.answer: It reads `cur->next` after `cur` was freed: a use-after-free, undefined behaviour. Swap the lines: `prev->next = cur->next;` first, then `free(cur);`.
quiz.explain: gcc warns `pointer 'cur' used after 'free'` and valgrind reports an invalid read. It might seem to work, but the freed memory may already be reused.

quiz.q: A function `void remove_value(struct node *head, int target)` removes the first node holding `target` correctly when it is in the middle, but the program misbehaves when the target is the first node. Why, and what is the usual fix?
quiz.answer: `head` is a copy of the caller's pointer. The function can free the first node and change its own `head`, but the caller's variable still points at the freed node (a dangling pointer). Fix: return the new head (`struct node *remove_value(...)`, called as `list = remove_value(list, x);`).
quiz.explain: Same reason a function cannot change an `int` argument (Day 11): parameters are copies.

quiz.q: `prev` and `cur` are adjacent nodes in a list `[a, ..., prev, cur, x, y]`. Which single statement removes `cur` from the list without losing `x` and `y`?
quiz.explain: Only C changes a link stored in the list. A cuts off `cur`, `x` and `y` (they leak). B and D only change local pointer variables; the list is unchanged. (After C, call `free(cur)`.)

write.prompt: Using `struct node { int elem; struct node *next; };`, write `struct node *remove_first(struct node *head, int target)`: it removes the first node whose `elem` is `target`, frees it, and returns the (possibly new) head. If no node holds `target` (or the list is empty), it changes nothing and returns `head`.
write.explain:
**Find.** `cur` starts at the head and `prev` at `NULL` (nothing is before the head). The loop condition tests `cur` first, so `cur->elem` is only read when `cur` is not `NULL` (`&&` stops early). Each step moves `prev` to `cur` and `cur` to the next node.

**Not found.** The loop ends with `cur == NULL` if the end was reached. This also covers the empty list (the loop never runs). Return `head` unchanged.

**Unlink.** If `prev` is still `NULL`, the walk stopped at the head: move the head to the second node (`NULL` if there is none). Otherwise make `prev` skip `cur`. When `cur` is the last node, `cur->next` is `NULL` and `prev` becomes the new last node: no extra case.

**Free.** Only after unlinking, because unlinking reads `cur->next`. Return `head`, since the caller's pointer must change when the head is removed. With the test `main` of the lesson (list `[10,20,30,40,50]`, removing 30, 10, 50, 99):

```
$ ./remove
[10,20,30,40,50]
[10,20,40,50]
[20,40,50]
[20,40]
[20,40]
```

valgrind reports `6 allocs, 6 frees`.

rubric.item: `prev = NULL`, `cur = head`; loop advances both, `prev` one step behind
loop condition tests `cur != NULL` before reading `cur->elem`
not found / empty list: returns `head` unchanged

pitfalls: `while (cur->elem != target && cur)`: tests `cur` too late, so the end of the list dereferences `NULL`.
Forgetting the head case: `prev->next` with `prev == NULL` crashes.
Returning nothing (`void`): the caller cannot see a new head.

write.prompt:
Complete this program that uses the notebook's generic stack (`qlgstack.h`). It pushes a heap **copy** of each word, prints the stack, pops the top word and prints it, and releases everything with no leaks. The output must be:

```
before: top : cat, bee, ant : bottom
popped cat
after: top : bee, ant : bottom
```

rubric.item: passes `print_string` (the function's name, no parentheses) to `qlgstack_print`
`free(top);` after printing, and `qlgstack_free(s, free_string);` at the end

pitfalls: `qlgstack_print(..., print_string(...))`: that CALLS the function; pass its name only.
Forgetting `free(top)`: pop frees only the node, so one word leaks.
`qlgstack_free(s, NULL)` here: the two remaining heap copies leak.

write.examNote: Modeled on the December 2016 final, Q5 (deleting a node from a linked list and returning its data), with a different node to delete.
write.prompt:
You are given these types:

```c
// A single node in a linked list
struct ListNode {
    int data;                  // the data in this node
    struct ListNode *next;     // pointer to the next node
};

// Refer to a linked list with a pointer to the first node
typedef struct ListNode *LinkedList;
```

The `next` pointer in the last node of a list is `NULL`.

Write a function with the header `int deleteLast(LinkedList list)` that deletes the **last** node of the list and returns the number that was inside it. It must also free the heap space used by the deleted node, so that there is no memory leak. If the list is empty or has only one node, the function must do nothing and return 0.

Example (`addToEnd` and `printList` are helper functions you do not write):

```
full list: [7,14,21,28,35]
deleted 35, list is [7,14,21,28]
deleted 28, list is [7,14,21]
deleted 21, list is [7,14]
deleted 14, list is [7]
deleted 0, list is [7]
```
write.explain: Verified with a test program (`addToEnd` appends a `malloc`'d node) that prints exactly the example output; valgrind reports `6 allocs, 6 frees` after `main` frees the last remaining node.

rubric.item: empty list and one-node list return 0 without changing anything, tested BEFORE using `list->next` / `list->next->next`
walks with a pointer to the node before the last (here `prev`/`cur`, stopping when `cur->next == NULL`)
saves the data of the last node before freeing it
sets the new last node's `next` to `NULL`
frees the deleted node and returns its data

pitfalls: Testing `list->next == NULL` before `list == NULL`: an empty list dereferences `NULL`.
`return cur->data;` after `free(cur)`: use-after-free. Save it first.
Freeing the last node but not setting `prev->next = NULL`: the list now ends in a dangling pointer, and the next call reads freed memory.
Walking until `cur == NULL`: then you have gone one step too far and lost the last node.
Trying to handle the one-node list by freeing `list`: the caller's pointer would dangle, which is why the question says to do nothing.
